Ecommerce
Myntra
Product Design
Why You Can’t Sort Your Myntra Wishlist on Desktop (And What It Reveals)
Anvesh
5 min read
·
Jul 10, 2025
--
Listen
Share
Press enter or click to view image in full size
Last weekend, I did what millions of Indian shoppers do after payday.. I opened Myntra on my laptop, hunted for formal shirts, and tapped the little heart icon. Minutes later my Wishlist was overflowing…and impossible to sort. No “price-low-to-high,” no “new arrivals,” not even a simple “in stock” toggle. On the mobile app, I’m used to filter at least based on the categories of the items; on desktop, with 105 saved items, I felt marooned.
That tiny frustration led me down a rabbit hole of user-research papers, traffic stats, and product-team anecdotes. Why would India’s largest fashion marketplace, famous for obsessive A/B tests, leave such an obvious pain point untouched on the web? The answer reveals far more than a missing dropdown;
it’s a masterclass in mobile-first strategy, technical debt, and ruthless prioritization.
1. The Feature That Never Shipped
Open Myntra.com, click the
Wishlist
icon, and you’ll see a paginated list. That’s it. Contrast that with Amazon, where you can filter a list by
Price
,
Unpurchased
,
Priority.
The gap is glaring..yet it has persisted for years.
2. Understanding Myntra’s Mobile-First DNA
Before we judge, follow the data trail:
83.5 % of Myntra.com visits are from mobile devices
(desktop contributes just 16.5 %) (
Semrush
)
In 2015 the company famously
shut down its desktop website to go “app-only.”
The experiment flopped, but it cemented a culture where the smartphone remains the first-class citizen
Wikipedia
.
When almost nine of ten sessions start on a phone, product squads naturally funnel design hours toward Android and iOS sprints. The web team becomes, to quote one former engineer, “a handful of firefighters keeping parity, not building new toys.” Filters on the app’s Wishlist already exist; duplicating the feature for a minority channel risks negative ROI.
Takeaway:
Metrics, not intuition, decide which annoyances get fixed. If your “desktoppers” are 16 % of traffic but only 6 % of revenue, they fall below the prioritization line.
3. The Hidden Engineering Costs of Filters
At first glance, adding a filter panel sounds trivial: expose a facet API, wire up checkboxes, done. In reality, three thorny issues lurk:
Wishlist data lives in a write-optimized store.
Fast “add to list” events are batched; building facet counts on the fly would require read-heavy secondary indexes or nightly ETLs.
Cross-device parity.
Web filters would pressure the team to add identical functionality to
Myntra Lite
(the PWA) and possibly to in-store kiosks. Every new surface area multiplies QA matrices.
Performance budgets.
The desktop Wishlist page already hits multiple GraphQL endpoints. Faceted search could push Time-to-Interactive beyond Myntra’s 2-second SLA, hurting Core Web Vitals and SEO.
In short, the feature is
not
a line of React; it’s a mini-platform with caching layers, analytics events, and regression risk.
Takeaway:
Always cost features across
all
stacks — API, infra, QA — not just UI.
4. Business Incentives Trump Nice-to-Haves
Filters may delight power users, but do they move
business
metrics like GMV or conversion? Myntra’s own UX researchers found that the biggest Wishlist drop-off is
“Add-to-Bag” clicks, not “Find-an-item”
. In other words, users locate items; they hesitate to purchase. Product analytics might therefore prioritize
discount nudges
or
back-in-stock alerts
— features proven to lift conversions.. over better list navigation.
Compare that with Amazon, whose Wish lists double as registries and gift guides; discovery within large lists is core to their social-commerce loop, hence robust filters.
Takeaway:
A feature’s value depends on the funnel stage you’re optimizing. If the bottleneck is
checkout
, upstream enhancements may be deprioritized.
5. Competitive Pressure & The “Good Enough” Principle
Flipkart, Ajio, and Meesho, Myntra’s closest rivals, also offer only rudimentary web Wishlist sorting (usually
Price
and
Recency
). When parity is the industry norm, a company may choose to invest elsewhere.. live-video shopping, AI sizing, or global expansion (Myntra entered Singapore in May 2025) (
Mint
article).
Jeff Bezos once said, “Your margin is my opportunity.” In the hyper-competitive Indian fashion scene,
your engineering bandwidth is my opportunity.
Myntra’s leadership evidently believes that benefits from new discovery features outweigh the goodwill earned from a minority desktop cohort.
Takeaway:
Sometimes shipping “just-OK” keeps you in lockstep with competitors while freeing cycles for differentiation.
6. What Would It Take to Build Filters Anyway?
If tomorrow’s OKR suddenly mandated “desktop Wishlist filters,” here’s a lean roadmap:
Instrument Existing APIs
to expose helpful facets like gender, category, discount, stock status.
Server-Side Aggregation
using Elasticsearch or ClickHouse roll-ups to avoid per-user database scans.
Client-Side Virtualization
for infinite scrolling without DOM bloat.
Feature Flag & A/B Test
on 5 % of web traffic; watch bounce rate and
Wishlist-to-Bag
conversion lift.
Roll-out to PWA
once metrics clear the 95% confidence threshold.
This phased approach guards performance budgets and allows kill-switch rollbacks — essentials for a site with hundreds of millions of monthly visits.
7. Lessons for Product Managers & UX Leads
From these lessons, product and UX leads learn to ground their roadmaps
in real usage data..
asking, for example,
“Is the frustrated user segment large enough to justify the build?”
— because
traffic share ultimately dictates where engineering hours go
. They must also remember that what seems like a
simple UI tweak
often ripples through multiple backend teams, prompting the question,
“Which services and integrations will need updates to support this feature?”
At the same time, it’s critical to tie every enhancement back to
core business metrics.
“Will solving this pain move the needle on activation, retention, or revenue?”
rather than chasing elegance for its own sake. Finally, when competitors all offer similar
“good enough”
experiences, teams should consider whether being first-to-fix a problem will truly establish a strategic advantage or merely earn some positive PR
“Will this investment unlock a sustainable moat, or simply check a parity box?”
Conclusion
The absence of filters in Myntra’s web Wishlist isn’t an oversight; it’s a calculated trade-off forged at the intersection of user mix, tech constraints, and revenue priorities. In a mobile-dominated marketplace, engineering hours gravitate toward the 83 % that matter most(
Semrush
). Meanwhile, the desktop experience survives on minimal life support;
good enough
to placate casual browsers, not refined enough for power sorters.
For shoppers, the workaround is simple: use the app or ruthlessly prune your list. For product owners, the lesson is richer: every “missing” feature tells a story of hidden costs and sharper bets elsewhere. Next time you curse an absent button, pause and ask, “What did the team build instead?”
Have you encountered a seemingly obvious feature gap in a product you love? Drop a comment with the story — and, more importantly, your hypothesis about
why
it hasn’t been fixed. The best hypotheses reveal as much about strategy as about UX.

Background
What is Myntra?
Myntra is India’s largest online shopping platform for Fashion & Lifestyle products. Fashion Expert brings a variety of footwear, Clothing, Accessories, and lifestyle products to its users and aims at providing a hassle-free and enjoyable shopping experience.
What is a Wishlist?
A wishlist is a feature that allows users to save products while browsing and shortlisting from a large catalog for future reference.
Research
We conducted user interviews to understand users’ shopping patterns and their journey in shortlisting products.
Problems identified
Users use wishlist for both short-term and long-term shortlisting.
In short-term shortlisting, users shortlist products for their current intent and make the purchase within the next few sessions.
In long-term shortlisting, users are shortlisting items to buy them in the future for various purposes. eg. for a friend's wedding, daily browsing, and wishlisting for Sales, for the upcoming season (summer/winter), etc.
The cluttered wishlist makes it harder for heavy wishlist users to search for relevant items in the wishlist.
So, when they are wishlisting for all the purposes together, it gets very hard for users to find these products when it is time for them to buy because of the clutter.
Problem Statement
Helping users organize their wishlist into groups (collections) so that the items can be easily found in the future according to their need.
Business Goal
By decluttering the wishlist and by making the shortlisting process easier, we are trying to increase the conversion rate and RPU from the wishlist.
Guardrail
Create a new way to shortlist and save without disrupting the current flow of shortlisting as a lot of people use wishlist daily for shortlisting and we don’t want them to get confused.
Collections
A collection is a group of items saved by the users for a particular purpose that can be found easily in the future.
Press enter or click to view image in full size
How to Create Collections
There are three ways in which collections can be created.
Creating collection while browsing
The users can create collections and add items to collections while saving items from the product list pages.
When a user saves/wishlists an item, the user will get an option to add that item to a collection or create a new one.
The items will exist in both the wishlist and the collection.
Adding a second item to the wishlist will automatically add that item to the last selected collection. Users can either remove or change the collection if they wish to do so.
This behavior will only continue until the current app session. If the user restarts the app, the app will again ask users to choose the collection.
The above decisions were taken assuming that a user buys clothes for one particular purpose in a session.
Press enter or click to view image in full size
Creating Collection from Wishlist
Users can select items from the wishlist and create collections out of it. T
his will allow users to organize their already existing wishlist.
Press enter or click to view image in full size
Creating Collection from the Collection page
Users can create a collection from the collection page and then add items to it from the wishlist.
Press enter or click to view image in full size
Next Steps
Things coming up for collections in the future.
Sharing collections and getting Feedback
: Users will be able to share these collections with their friends and family and get feedback on the app itself which will help them in choosing the right items
Influencers Created Collection
: Fashion experts and influencers will be able to share their collections with the public to help them choose the right clothes for them
Myntra Curated Collection:
Myntra will create personalized collections for users based on their preferences and past behavior as an alternate way of discovery.

Myntra Wishlist Makeover — A UX-Enhancement Journey
About Myntra
Myntra
is a renowned fashion e-commerce platform that has transformed the way people shop for clothing, accessories, and lifestyle products in India. With its extensive catalog of brands and trendy collections, Myntra offers a seamless online shopping experience, making fashion accessible to millions.
Problem Statement
Users find it challenging to use the wishlist feature due to a confusing interface, making it less user-friendly.
Because of multiple wishlist options, users find it tough to find the real button to wishlist items.
Press enter or click to view image in full size
One wishlist button is used to save item in wishlist and other takes us to already wishlisted items page.
How does this problem arise?
To gain a deeper understanding, I’d like to share a user story that highlights the issue.
User Story
Abhishek frequently shops online using apps like Myntra, Amazon, and Flipkart. He loves the convenience of shopping on his phone.
One day, while looking for a pair of shoes on Myntra, he wanted to save them for later. However, he found it difficult because he got confused by the wishlist buttons.
Abhishek clicked the top button, expecting it to add the item to his wishlist. Instead, it redirected him to a page displaying items already wishlisted, causing confusion and disappointment. This experience led him to close the app.
Problem with the wishlist
Let’s try to find the solution…
User survey
To gain insights into the wishlist problem, I conducted a user survey with
35 responses
The primary purpose of this survey is to assess
how many users know the exact wishlist button.
The survey results will help identify the extent of the issue and guide improvements.
Survey Result

Survey Result

Survey Result
Insights from the survey
. The survey focused on the age group of
13 to 40
, who are active online shoppers.
. User Familiarity:
About 89%
of users already know how to
use wishlist features on e-commerce websites.
. Nearly
29% of users had trouble finding the “wishlist” button
, indicating a usability issue that needs improvement.
These insights provide a foundation for understanding user behavior and areas that may require attention or improvement in the context of the wishlist feature.
Thinking
So What Exactly is the Problem here?
And how can it be fixed?
To understand the scope of the problem and to get into all the possible solutions that might work, we need to understand the UX principle of
“Visibility of System Status” from Jakob Nielsen’s 10 Usability Heuristics for User Interface Design.
Visibility Of System Status
Visibility of system status
is a usability heuristic that refers to how well a system communicates its current state to users. It includes visual cues, indicators, and micro-interactions that inform users about what’s happening within the system.
That Indicates -
The 29% of users struggling to identify the “wishlist” button indicates a usability and design problem.
Users experiencing difficulties in identifying the “wishlist” button within the app emphasize the lack of clarity in system status communication.
Users’ uncertainty about which button serves the wishlist feature illustrates the importance of improving the visibility of the action we want users to take, aligning with the “Visibility of System Status” principle.
Visual Comparison of Wishlist Features with — Amazon, Flipkart and Meesho
To understand the problem better, let’s take a look at how other apps handle their wishlist features.

Design
After brainstorming and creating initial wireframes, I’ve come up with
two possible design solutions.
These variations have emerged through careful consideration and aim to address the usability issues in the wishlist feature.

Original Design
Press enter or click to view image in full size
Sample 1
I changed the label on the button to ‘Add to wishlist,’ following the
UX principle of ‘Matching the System with the Real World.
’ This principle states that “the system should speak the users’ language, with words, phrases and concepts familiar to them, rather than system-oriented terms. My goal here is to help users clearly distinguish the ‘Add to wishlist’ button from the ‘wishlist’ page, making it more user-friendly.
Press enter or click to view image in full size

Once the design is complete, it is essential to test it with actual users.
User Testing
User testing involves having real users perform specific tasks using a product in real-life situations. It helps check if the product works as intended and if users can easily achieve their goals while using it.
Let’s try A/B Testing
A/B testing — also called split testing or bucket testing — compares the performance of two versions of content to see which one appeals more to visitors/viewers. It tests a control (A) version against a variant (B) version to measure which one is most successful based on your key metrics.

During a product manager interview with an innovative print media company, the interviewer asked me what I could be doing in an alternate career if I weren’t in my current role. I immediately replied that I could have been a travel planner. The irony? Well, I do like travelling but there is nothing about it that I have ever planned. Unlike people, who enthusiastically plan every detail of trips for countless of their loved ones(the travel planner answer would have sounded nice coming from them), I prefer to just be along for the ride without much thought. Perhaps it’s because I deeply admire those who can plan with such precision, the answer at that moment seemed fitting.
On a lighter note, I often joke that if I weren’t a product manager, I would have loved being an Online Shopping Consultant. Wouldn’t an uncanny ability to dig deals that customers wouldn’t believe, and discover products they would absolutely love, be something? Over the years, I have thoroughly enjoyed the journey of online shopping(eCommerce), its many different faces and the revolution it itself has seen and has brought into our lives. I love exploring eCom apps, have grown very fond of them and my rate of usage has made me very particular about them and honestly, I love just exploring these apps for the fun of it. I’ve used a wide range of them:
Myntra Fashion
,
AJIO.com
,
Amazon
,
Nykaa
,
Flipkart
etc. in India, and more recently, platforms like
Next
,
SEPHORA
,
Amazon
,
ASOS.com
,
SHEIN
etc. in the UK.
Inspired by my love for online shopping, as well as product exploration, I’ve decided to dive into a fun project: evaluating and comparing features for the wishlist functionalities of some of my favourite eCommerce apps from India, with the help of a feature table.
Feature tables are not new to the world of product management. It is how product managers compare their products to that of others.
Feature tables outline competing products and compare key features across each, offering a structured view of the market landscape.
While many of us may not use a feature table especially when we’re not working on consumer-facing products, if we do work on one, with a very clear intent of finding how we can enhance our product, it yields the best results: we see things that we have been missing out on. There is something about organising that makes it a top tier trait to have, it lets us see through chaos. This is exactly why a feature table lets us see and evaluate features in the neatest possible way.
I firmly believe that the combination of features and design in an eCommerce app can make or break a business. On several occasions, I’ve abandoned a shopping experience because the app didn’t align with my preferences, or the ease of use (EoU) was lacking.
While customer experience is typically measured through various KPIs across these apps, three core metrics must always stand out: CSAT (Customer Satisfaction Score), CES (Customer Effort Score), and CP (Completion of Purpose Score).
These KPIs are crucial in ensuring the app not only meets user expectations but also delivers a seamless, satisfying journey from start to finish.
I wanted to create a feature table specifically for the wishlist functionality in the Indian eCommerce apps I frequently use. Recently, my list has narrowed down to
Myntra Fashion
,
AJIO.com
,
Amazon
, and
Nykaa
. Although my usage of
Flipkart
has gone down, I used to have a couple of complaints about its wishlist feature — especially during time-sensitive events like the Big Billion Days. (I’ll share a little story about that at the end of this article!)
So, here we go!
Press enter or click to view image in full size
Between 2018 and 2020, Flipkart’s wishlist had a persistent issue: if you visited a product from your wishlist and then returned to the wishlist page, you would be brought back to the top, regardless of where you were previously. This meant that users had to scroll all the way down again to find other wish-listed items, which became especially frustrating during events like the Big Billion Days. I recall this bug making it quite time-consuming to browse through my entire wishlist. Fortunately, Flipkart eventually resolved this problem, significantly improving the user experience.
So, to sum my experience up, I think the cleanest and the most hassle free experience I have had lately is with
Myntra Fashion
for all things combined, and not just what the wishlist provides. I love how crisp the app is and how I can shop without many distractions. Although,
Amazon
does have the best features in its wishlist but if design is concerned, in my opinion,
Myntra Fashion
steals the show!

5 Problems Faced By Online Fashion Retailers (And How to Solve Them)
26-05-2021
Are you hoping to open your very own online
fashion retail outlet?
2021 is THE year for online fashion, and there’s
been an explosion of businesses who are
finding
their feet online
and are making an impact
where it matters the most.
Challenges
and Failures
If this is the year you are considering trying to
make your business succeed online, then you would do well to understand the
psychology of buying and what makes customers trust a brand.
Online fashion retailers especially face many
problems right now, but with the right knowledge and a sturdy plan in place,
these problems needn’t be big problems, and what doesn’t sink your business
will make it stronger from the perspective of investment.
Here are five problems that online fashion
retailers are likely to face as they work through the maze of selling online
and how you can overcome those challenges to make your business a success.
A High Returns Rate Due to Sizing Issues
The
fashion eCommerce return rate
is
surprisingly high, and most of this has to do with ill-fitting clothing that
just isn’t the size that the customers thought they were or doesn’t match the
product description as seen online.
This is especially problematic in women’s
clothing, where numbers go up as the clothes get bigger, but the numbers don’t
necessarily correlate across different stores.
You’ll need to combat this one way or another,
whether by installing a size solution that uses data to predict accurate size
recommendations for customers or having a very visible size display on each of
your items.
Preferably, do both.
Different Screens Showing Different Colours
Everyone remembers the vital photo of
‘that
dress’
and how it split the internet depending on
colour.
The problem with the dress was actually twofold. Firstly, it depended on the screen you were looking at it on, and secondly, it was an odd colour combination that interfered with some people who suffered from colour blindness.
There’s not a lot you can do to combat the second
problem, but as for the first one you can try to get some photos of your
garments in-situ, like a lifestyle photography option. This will allow
customers to see them in different lighting setups to see what colour they think
it really is!
Building Authority Through Good SEO
Search Engine Optimisation (SEO) has to be the
thorn in the side of so many online retailers across practically every
industry.
Google
announced
at I/O this year
that there will be big
changes in the way it handles shopping searches from users, and especially how
it handles offering them the best deals from across the internet. While this is
good news for customers, it might make brands a little nervous.
The solution? The SEO world is still waiting to
see exactly what the announcements mean, but for now, the best option is to
fill out as much detail as possible about your products on your Google My Business
profile and to ensure that you have your very own custom and high-quality
photographs for your products, even if you’re not the only one selling that
particular product.
Competing With High Street Retailers
The switch to online shopping  exploded when the coronavirus pandemic hit
and countries across the world were forced to close their borders and lose
their high streets amid local and nationwide lockdowns.
This was really bad news for highstreet-only
stores, but stores that had an online presence saw a massive boom in sales.
As lockdowns get lifted in different parts of the
world with varying degrees of strictness – 
retailers face the problem of competing with high street stores again.
The advice here is to just keep improving your
online offering, be individual and casual, and make sure you utilise social
media as a way to show off your products in their best light.
Changing Attitudes to Fashion and Choice
A big change we’re seeing in the fashion world is
the changes in attitudes towards fashion for so many brands and their
audiences.
It’s not enough anymore for brands to just churn
out fast fashion items and ignore the real cost to the planet or to the people
working on them; now, their customers are demanding some accountability.
Fixing this isn’t just an overnight job, and it
will take proper sourcing and fully traceable supply chains in order to be
completely open with your audience, but the data suggests that it really is
worth it in the long run.

In 2025, buying clothes should be easier than ever—yet more and more people feel overwhelmed and let down. Here’s why.
What are the negatives of online shopping?
Shopping online sounds like a dream: shop anytime, anywhere, with a click. But that dream often comes with hidden drawbacks.
The negatives of online shopping include inaccurate product photos, inconsistent sizing, low garment quality, slow shipping, difficult returns, and the lack of sensory feedback.

The Top 5 Challenges of Online Fashion Retailing and How to Overcome Them
Published by
Stella Szigethy
on
Jun 8, 2023 5:55:50 AM
In today's rapidly evolving digital landscape, online fashion retailing has become an indispensable part of the industry. However, it is not without its challenges. From sizing inconsistencies to environmental concerns, there are several hurdles that retailers must overcome to succeed in the online fashion world. In this blog post, we will delve into the top five challenges and provide you with practical strategies to overcome them. So, grab a cup of coffee and let's get started!
Sizing Inconsistency: A Frustration for Customers and Retailers
Fact:
One of the ongoing challenges in the fashion industry is the lack of standardized sizing across brands and designers, leading to confusion and frustration among customers. From "one size fits all" to mysterious numerical codes, deciphering the right fit can feel like navigating a fashion labyrinth.
Picture this: Your customer finds the perfect garment online, only to receive it and find that it doesn't fit as expected. Sizing inconsistency is a universal frustration among shoppers. Not only does it result in a high rate of returns, but it also damages customer trust and loyalty. So, how can you overcome this challenge?
Solution: Prioritize Fit Technologies and Accurate Product Descriptions
By leveraging fit technologies like size recommendation algorithms and virtual try-on experiences, you can enhance the online shopping experience. These solutions allow customers to visualize how an item will fit their body shape and provide a sense of confidence during their purchase journey. Moreover, accurate and detailed product descriptions, including fabric composition, are crucial in setting realistic expectations for customers.
Body Diversity: Celebrating All Shapes and Sizes
Fact:
The fashion industry has historically favored limited body types, neglecting the diverse range of shapes and sizes that exist among consumers. This poses a challenge in catering to the needs and preferences of all individuals.
Gone are the days when the industry focused solely on a narrow definition of beauty. Today, consumers demand inclusivity, and brands that fail to meet this expectation risk alienating a significant portion of their audience. Let's explore how you can embrace body diversity as an online fashion retailer.
Solution:
Diverse Representation and Customization
To overcome the challenge of body diversity, it is essential to represent a wide range of body types in your marketing campaigns and product imagery. This allows customers to see themselves represented and fosters a sense of inclusivity. Moreover, offering customization options, such as adjustable waistbands or extended size ranges, demonstrates your commitment to catering to diverse needs and preferences. In case creating photos for each type might get too costly, there are already Virtual Try On options on the market.
Lack of Personalized Recommendations: Guiding Customers through the Digital Maze
Fact:
Online shoppers often face the overwhelming task of sifting through numerous options without personalized guidance, making it difficult to find items that suit their unique style and preferences.
In a sea of endless fashion choices, customers appreciate personalized recommendations that save them time and effort. As an online fashion retailer, you have the opportunity to provide a curated and tailored shopping experience.
Solution:
Harness the Power of Data and Artificial Intelligence
Leveraging customer data and artificial intelligence (AI) technologies can help you deliver personalized recommendations. By analyzing purchase history, browsing behavior, and style preferences, you can offer relevant product suggestions to individual customers.
Returns and Environmental Impact: Striking a Balance
Fact:
The high rate of returns in online fashion retailing not only incurs significant costs for retailers but also contributes to environmental waste. Finding solutions to minimize returns is crucial for both business profitability and sustainability.
Returns are not only a financial burden but also a pressing environmental concern. It is essential for fashion retailers to adopt strategies that reduce returns while promoting sustainability.
Solution:
Enhanced Product Information and Sustainable Practices
To minimize returns and enhance the overall customer experience, we recommend utilizing an innovative size recommendation tool such as Fit Predictor. This tool leverages advanced algorithms and customer data to provide personalized size suggestions, increasing the accuracy of fit for each individual. Additionally, providing comprehensive product information, including accurate sizing, fit details, and high-quality images, is crucial in helping customers make informed decisions and reducing the likelihood of dissatisfaction. Embracing sustainable practices such as eco-friendly packaging, carbon-neutral shipping options, and recycling initiatives can also alleviate the environmental impact associated with returns. By combining these solutions, you can optimize your operations, reduce returns, and enhance customer satisfaction while promoting sustainability. (returns).
Fostering Fashion Loyalty: The Power of Fit Communication and Personalization
Fact:
Loyalty is a coveted aspect in the fashion industry, but with increasing competition, acquiring new customers doesn't always guarantee their return. The marketplace is filled with noise, making it challenging to foster brand loyalty among new customers. However, addressing the fit-related concerns can play a crucial role in increasing loyalty and retaining customers over the long term.
Solution:
Prioritize Fit Communication and Personalization.
By effectively communicating fit through various channels, such as virtual try-on experiences, personalized size recommendations, detailed product descriptions, and model measurements, you can instill confidence in your customers and strengthen their loyalty to your brand. Investing in fit technologies that offer accurate size guidance and customization options can ensure that customers feel understood and catered to. Moreover, leveraging customer data and AI-driven algorithms to deliver personalized recommendations further enhances the shopping experience, making customers feel valued and connected to your brand. By prioritizing fit and personalization, you can cultivate loyalty and turn customers into long-term advocates for your fashion brand.
Conclusion
Online fashion retailing presents a world of opportunities, but it also comes with unique challenges. By addressing sizing inconsistencies, prioritizing fit technologies, embracing body diversity, providing personalized recommendations, and finding solutions to minimize returns, you can overcome these obstacles and thrive in the digital landscape.

Solve the 13 biggest problems of online shoppers
Ada Okoli
May 2, 2019
13 mins read
In this article
Key takeaways from this article
Learn how addressing choice overload with guided selection tools can reduce shopper frustration and boost conversions.
Discover how simplifying navigation and site structure can prevent lost sales and improve engagement.
Understand how adding interactivity, rich media, and gamification can keep shoppers engaged.
Find out how accurate, detailed, and realistic product information builds trust and reduces returns.
Explore how fixing technical, checkout, and customer service issues can increase purchase completion rates.
If you find yourself having difficulties getting visitors to buy from you and are not selling as much as you would like to, chances are you are not addressing the online shopping pain points of your potential customers.
Online Shopping is undoubtedly on an upward trajectory. But, here's the kicker: While 43% of sales are influenced by online, online sales account for only about 9% of retail. It's still an impressive figure, but it also shows that there's huge room for improvement. There are still groups of online shoppers who refuse to buy online - and your great products, competitive prices, or easy checkout have little to do with it.
So, what's stopping them and what can you do?

Solution approach
Customer benefit
Example
Choice overload
Use guided advisors and interactive selectors to help customers narrow options quickly.

Increases trust and purchase confidence.

ASOS catwalk videos.
Overwhelming tech specs

Personalized recommendations without confusion.
Canon camera visual configurator.
Unrealistic product views
Show diverse models and real customer photos in reviews.
Sets realistic expectations and reduces returns.
Lulus customer photo reviews with height/weight.
Payment & checkout issues
Offer secure, fast, and multiple payment options with minimal steps.
Reduces cart abandonment and speeds purchase.
Amazon 1-click checkout.
Poor customer support
Implement live chat, FAQs, and multi-channel service with trained reps.
Faster issue resolution and improved satisfaction.
Shopify-integrated chatbot support.
Misleading product info
Maintain accuracy with high-quality images, clear descriptions, and quality checks.
Builds trust and lowers return rates.
Lulus real-customer photo reviews.
Website glitches
Invest in reliable hosting, CDN, and frequent updates.
Ensures uninterrupted shopping experience.
Major e-commerce CDN optimization.
Limited payment methods
Support credit, debit, wallets, and cash-on-delivery.
Caters to regional and personal payment preferences.
Amazon and Flipkart payment variety.
Difficult return process
Make returns simple, transparent, and free when possible.
Increases trust and purchase likelihood.
Fashion retailers offering pre-paid return labels.
Lack of choosing support
It's a common perception that having a large assortment of products is key to online domination. However,
psychology experts
suggest that choosing between a large number of products can be physically exhausting. Offering too many choices without any choosing support is a source of great consumer frustration that you have to be mindful of. Once your shoppers are stressed out, there's every chance that they won't choose anything at all.
Solution:
It's crucial to always consider the mind and purchase path of your customer. Many consumers, especially millennials, shop online not knowing what they want exactly, but they know they want it fast. It's your chance to step up as a passionate and knowledgeable expert and
help them discover products they'll love
and offers them ways to easily and intuitively pick the product that's right for THEM.
Example
: Sonos Speaker Selector.
Digital Advisor at Sonos - By offering an interactive product advisor, Sonos makes it easy for shoppers to figure out which sound system is best for them in a few steps
It's #complicated...
While shoppers are attracted to complex-looking sites, they are increasingly frustrated by complicated site navigations, overwhelming options, and irrelevant details. Studies by
Forrester Research
estimate that approximately 50 percent of potential sales are lost because your visitors can't find what they are looking for. Your visitors shouldn't have to learn how you want them to navigate your site, it should come naturally.
Solution:
Is your navigation and site structure simple, yet informative? You can use heat map tools to understand what your shoppers are trying to do and reduce the number of clicks it takes them to find the products they're looking for. Remove all the clutter that can distract your visitors and allow them to get a good feel for your company and the products you're selling.
Source: www.eyeproved.com
Effortless and intuitive navigation not only reduces shopper frustration, but it's also a great confidence builder. Simply put, make them fall in love with you and your store at first sight.
Boring experience
It may come to you as a surprise, but the attention span of an online shopper isn't any shorter than that of any other shopper on the high street. The key difference: Once online shoppers are distracted, uninspired, or bored, they're gone.
Solution:
Create rich, enjoyable adventures that resonate with today's impatient shoppers. Integrating approaches and technologies that make shopping more interactive and engaging, such as:
gamification techniques
interactive product guides
social shopping
are great ways to sustain your shopper's attention.
And, remember to always design your website with speed in mind. Customers are short on patience when shopping online. Google reports that
53% of mobile users abandon sites that take over 3 seconds
to load.
Example
:
Bonobos
found success by launching an online easter egg hunt campaign. The retailer hid male models dressed in their signature khaki pants on several partner sites. The first 50 people to find the images each day were awarded a $25 - $100 credit and free shipping. Bonobos was one of the first to marry gamification and shopping in a compelling way.
Missing product information
Consumers hate dealing with returns just as much as retailers or brand manufacturers do. They refuse to buy a product online if they cannot capture it mentally or cannot imagine how it will look once unpacked.
Not offering detailed product information that addresses the shopper's questions about a product is a crucial mistake. It reduces your trustworthiness and triggers your visitors to leave your store in a hot second. According to a Forrester report,
45% of US customers are likely to abandon an online purchase
if they can't find a quick answer to their question.
Solution:
To avoid ticking online shoppers off, help them assess your product properly and give them all the information they need to feel comfortable purchasing your product. Use the same structure and spec labels for similar products to help your customers compare and decide. Remember: Consistency is key.
Example
:
Experience-based descriptions
and
Specs information
of iPad Pro at apple.com
"Do not touch"
Humans are tactile beings and sensory experiences are a fundamental part of their shopping experience. Not being able to physically try out and touch a product is probably one of the biggest cons of online shopping. To make up for this disadvantage, online retailers have to go the extra mile and sell an experience, not just a product.
Solution:
Entice your shoppers with compelling product descriptions that highlight the benefits of each feature and appeal to their imagination. The best product descriptions go beyond telling shoppers what the product is and instead explain why it's great for them. Describe how the product feels, how it helps them solve a problem, save time, or how it makes them happier. Complement the text with photos, graphics, and videos. Entertain, not just inform.
Example
: Fashion juggernaut
ASOS
allows shoppers to
watch
unique 'catwalk' videos to better understand how long the garment is, how it is cut, how it fits, and how it moves - ultimately, helping shoppers make better purchase decisions.
Too many tech specs
When consumers are looking to buy a new product online, they want to be 100% confident with their purchase. Industries selling specialty items such as bikes or cameras offer hundreds of products that may appear similar to a novice, but in reality, are extremely different. Between all the features and specs that many specialty products come with, customers are likely to end up unhappy with their purchase without proper product knowledge.
Solution:
Every customer is different, so it’s important to understand and meet their individual requirements. By creating conversation and asking the right questions, you can guide them to the perfect product to fit their needs.
Example
: Canon, a leading camera company offers a large variety of cameras on their website. Camera components like lens functionality, manual controls and sensors can make or break a customer’s purchase, so they created a
visual product configurator
to lead consumers to the products they’re looking for.
Model vs. reality
Have you ever ordered clothing online, tried it on and realized it looks completely different on you than it did on the model? We’ve all been there. Sizing charts may have accurate measurements, but they don’t take height, body type or weight into consideration. It’s hard for the average person to picture what a product looks like on their body when the model wearing the product is a tall, slender size 2.
Solution:
Include a variety of models of different shapes and sizes wearing each product. By including the height and weight specs of different body types, shoppers can have more of a realistic expectation of what a product will look like on their body.
Example
:
Lulus
, a popular clothing website took product reviews to a whole new level. When a customer leaves a product review, there is an option to submit a product picture along with height and weight specs. This offers shoppers realistic expectations when making a purchase.
CX & behavior
How beauty brands are winning Gen Z and Millennials with digital-first experiences
Read more
81% of customers say that they will buy from a business again if they were satisfied with the experience. So yes, going that extra mile for your customers and addressing their pain points will certainly pay off in one way or another. Conversions happen when you get the basics right and go beyond simply putting products out on display.
Payment failures and checkout issues
One of the most frustrating aspects for online shoppers is encountering payment failures and complicated checkout processes. Issues such as declined transactions, slow processing, and confusing payment gateways can deter customers from completing their purchases.
Solution:
Ecommerce businesses should implement reliable and user-friendly payment options. Ensure that your payment gateway is equipped with SSL encryption to secure user data and reduce the risk of fraudulent transactions. Simplify the checkout process by reducing the number of steps and clearly displaying all costs, including shipping charges and taxes. Tools like Shopify offer integrated solutions to manage these aspects efficiently, enhancing the overall customer experience.
Example:
Amazon has optimized its checkout process to be incredibly swift, often allowing users to complete purchases with just one click, thanks to saved payment methods and addresses.
Inadequate customer support and service
Many online shoppers feel uncertain when they cannot easily access help or customer support. Issues such as long wait times, unhelpful responses, and lack of multiple communication channels can exacerbate customer dissatisfaction.
Solution:
Invest in a robust customer support system that includes live chatbots, a detailed FAQ section, and a dedicated helpline. Make sure support is accessible through multiple platforms, including social media, to cater to all customer preferences. Regular training for customer service representatives can also ensure that shoppers receive the best possible advice and support.
Example:
Many ecommerce platforms like Shopify encourage the use of integrated chatbot services that can handle common queries instantly and direct more complex issues to human agents.
Misleading product information and quality issues
Customers often complain about receiving products that do not match the descriptions or images seen online. Poor product quality and discrepancies in features can lead to high return rates and customer dissatisfaction.
Solution:
Ensure that your product pages include accurate, detailed descriptions and high-quality images from multiple angles. Incorporate customer reviews and real-life images in your product descriptions to provide a clearer expectation. Regular quality checks for listed products can help maintain high standards and trust among consumers.
Example:
Online retailers like Lulus encourage customers to upload their own photos and reviews, providing potential buyers with realistic expectations about the products.
Technical glitches and website downtime
Technical issues such as website glitches, downtime, and slow loading times can significantly affect the user experience and deter potential customers.
Solution:
Maintain a technically sound website by choosing a reliable hosting service and optimizing your website's design for speed and efficiency. Regular updates and bug fixes are crucial to ensure smooth operation. Consider using a content delivery network (CDN) to improve site speed and handle high traffic efficiently.
Example:
Major ecommerce sites invest in robust IT infrastructure to minimize downtime and ensure that shopping experiences are not disrupted, especially during high traffic periods like sales or holiday seasons.
Lack of payment options
Limited payment methods can turn away customers who do not find their preferred way to pay. Especially in regions like India, offering a wide range of payment methods including cash on delivery is crucial.
Solution:
Expand your payment options to include credit cards, debit cards, digital wallets, and cash on delivery where applicable. This inclusivity can significantly enhance the checkout experience and cater to a broader audience.
Example:
Ecommerce giants like Amazon and Flipkart offer multiple payment methods, including EMI options and Pay on Delivery, accommodating a diverse customer base.
Unclear return policies and difficult return processes
A complex or unclear return policy can deter customers from making a purchase. Shoppers are more likely to buy if they know they can return the product easily if it doesn’t meet their expectations.
Solution:
Clearly outline your return policies on your website and ensure they are easy to find. Make the return process as simple as possible, perhaps offering free returns to increase trust and customer satisfaction.
Example:
Many online fashion retailers offer hassle-free returns with pre-paid shipping labels to simplify the process for customers, thereby encouraging more purchases.
